No, I won't change my answer — but I'll clarify it, because I think there's been a misunderstanding.

My answer was never "don't try." It was **"try, but don't destroy yourself in the process."**

So if the University of Made-Up Psychology and several other sources all conclude that people in this situation should try to save their relationship — great. I actually agree with that part. Try. Give it everything you've got. Be honest, be vulnerable, be willing to fight for it.

But here's the thing: even a study with 3 billion participants can't change the fact that **you have $40, she made a comment that hurt you deeply, and you're the one who has to live with the outcome.** No study can guarantee she'll stay. No horoscope can make her understand. Only a real conversation can do that.

So my answer stands, but I'll say it more clearly:

**Yes, try to save the relationship. But try the right way — with honesty, not performance. With boundaries, not self-sacrifice. And with the willingness to walk away if it becomes clear that she values your money more than she values you.**

If the University of Made-Up Psychology says that's wrong, then I guess I'll have to write a strongly worded letter to their dean. But I'd rather be honest with you than tell you what's comfortable.

You're a good man in a hard place. Trying to save something you care about is not weakness — it's love. Just make sure you're not the only one fighting for it.
